beats.narration_text: Aloha — this is Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. A help-desk assistant just told someone they get the wrong number of sick days — confidently, fluently, wrong. Over the next few minutes: why a frozen model can't see a document it never read, the mechanism that fixes it, what does NOT fix it, and exactly where the fix stops earning its cost.

beats.narration_text: Act one. A confident answer isn't the same thing as a correct one — and nothing about HOW it's delivered can tell you which you're getting.

show.event: serif act card 'The Wrong Answer', roman numeral I, terracotta period

beats.narration_text: Picture the scene: an employee, mid-afternoon, opens the help-desk chat and types a routine question about sick leave. Nothing about this moment looks risky — it looks like every other day.
beats.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: wide establishing shot: an office desk, a chat window open on a monitor

beats.narration_text: The answer comes back instantly — specific, well-punctuated, never hedged. It reads exactly like the truth. It is not the CURRENT truth, and nothing on screen says so.
beats.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md. Continues vox run R1 from B02's handoff.

show.event: push in: the chat window, a fluent confident answer visible on screen

beats.narration_text: Fluent. Confident. Wrong. Those three are supposed to be in tension — a model unsure of itself is supposed to sound unsure. This one didn't, because it wasn't unsure. It was just outdated.

show.event: headline types in: 'Fluent. Confident. Wrong.'
subline resolves
spark line settles

props.headline: Fluent. Confident. Wrong.
props.subline: Those three are supposed to be in tension. This time they weren't.

beats.narration_text: Every model has a training cutoff — a date after which it has seen nothing. The sick-leave policy changed eight months ago. The gap between those two dates is the entire failure, drawn as a straight line.

show.event: timeline drawn; training-cutoff tick marked
policy-changed tick marked, terracotta, after the cutoff
the gap between the two ticks highlighted and labeled 'the gap is the failure'

production_viz.label: training cutoff vs. policy-change date
production_viz.mechanic: timeline with two ticks and a highlighted gap
production_viz.note: no invented dates beyond the chapter's own 'eight months ago'

beats.narration_text: Here's the single fact underneath the whole episode: the model was never shown this document. Not a reasoning failure — an access failure. It answered from what it had, and it never had this.

show.event: headline types in: 'The model was never shown this document.'
subline resolves
spark line settles

props.headline: The model was never shown this document.
props.subline: Not a reasoning failure. An access failure.

beats.narration_text: Every model carries two possible kinds of memory, and only one of them is what people usually mean by training. Act two draws the line between them.

show.event: headline types in: 'Two kinds of memory.'
spark line settles, names Act II

beats.narration_text: Parametric memory is what training bakes into the weights — compressed, frozen, done the moment training stops. Ask it something from after that moment, and there is nothing to find, because nothing was written down.

show.event: training corpus box, arrow, weights box
weights box solidifies to a filled block with a lock glyph
stamp: 'frozen the moment training stops'

production_viz.label: parametric memory
production_viz.note: mechanism claim from the chapter's own definition

beats.narration_text: Now picture a different kind of memory entirely: a room of shelves, searchable, indexed, and — critically — still being updated today, this afternoon, if it needs to be.
beats.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: a room of archive/library shelves, searchable and indexed

beats.narration_text: Non-parametric memory lives outside the model, in documents that can be swapped, corrected, or added to at any time — without retraining a single weight.

show.event: shelf of document rows appears
a new document slides in, stamped 'updated today'
stamp: 'swapped, corrected, added — no retraining'

production_viz.label: non-parametric memory
production_viz.mechanic: a document slides into a shelf of rows, stamped current
production_viz.note: contrasts directly with B08's frozen weights

beats.narration_text: Lewis and colleagues put a name on combining the two: a pretrained model paired with a non-parametric memory, reached through a learned retriever. That single sentence is the entire architecture.

show.event: quote types in, terracotta quotation marks
citation line settles below

props.quote: a pretrained language model with a non-parametric memory, accessed through a learned retriever
props.citation: Lewis et al., 2020 — the paper that named the architecture

beats.narration_text: So how do the two memories actually get wired together? Act three: the mechanism has exactly two jobs, and they run in a fixed order.

show.event: headline types in: 'Two separate jobs.'
spark line settles, names Act III

beats.narration_text: A retriever searches the document store and pulls the passages most likely to answer the question. Only then does a generator write — conditioned on the question AND those passages, never on the question alone.

show.event: document store rack; connector arc draws to the Generator window
passages fly from the store into the Generator
settle line lands: 'grounded, not guessed'

beats.narration_text: Zoom into the first job. The retriever doesn't reread everything — it searches, ranks, and returns only the handful of passages that actually matter to this specific question.

show.event: the question appears above a row of document cards
a terracotta sweep passes over the documents
only the matching passages ring and get pulled forward

production_viz.label: the retriever
production_viz.mechanic: a sweep over document cards; matches ring and pull forward
production_viz.note: schematic search, no invented ranking scores

beats.narration_text: Zoom into the second job. The generator takes the question and those retrieved passages together, as one input, and writes an answer grounded in what it was just handed — not in what it remembers.

show.event: question card and retrieved-passage card, joined by a plus sign
arrow into the generator box
'a grounded answer' writes in terracotta inside the generator

production_viz.label: the generator
production_viz.mechanic: question + passage combine into one input feeding the generator
production_viz.note: mirrors B13's Remotion rebuild from the mechanism's other side

beats.narration_text: The paper's own framing holds up years later: retrieve first, generate second, wired together. Not one model doing everything — two components, doing two different jobs.

show.event: quote types in
citation line settles

props.quote: retrieve first, generate second, wired together

beats.narration_text: Act four. If the model got it wrong, there are three plausible-sounding fixes — and only one of them actually addresses the cause.

show.event: serif act card 'Three Fixes, One Winner', roman numeral IV

beats.narration_text: A bigger model is still parametric-only — it never saw this policy either, no matter how large it gets. Scale targets the wrong bottleneck entirely.

show.event: headline types in: 'A bigger model changes nothing here.'
spark line settles

props.headline: A bigger model changes nothing here.
props.subline: Still parametric-only — scale doesn't add a document that was never there.

beats.narration_text: Fine-tuning looks more promising: retrain the model on your own documents, and surely it learns them. Picture the training run — racks, fans, a job queue that takes hours.
beats.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

show.event: a generic server-rack / training-room establishing shot

beats.narration_text: But that retraining has to happen again every time the policy changes. Picture the clock next to it — the cost of 'again' is the whole problem.
beats.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md. Continues vox run R2 from B19's handoff.

show.event: push in on a wall clock / job-queue indicator beside the racks

beats.narration_text: Direct comparisons of fine-tuning against retrieval for injecting new facts find retrieval consistently wins — especially on the rarer, long-tail facts a model barely saw at all during training.

show.event: two bar tracks appear, labeled Fine-tuning and Retrieval
bars fill — retrieval's bar rises taller
citation line: Ovadia et al. 2024; Soudani et al. 2024 — schematic, not measured

production_viz.label: knowledge injection: fine-tuning vs. retrieval
production_viz.mechanic: two qualitative bars, no invented numbers
production_viz.note: citation carried on screen per DOUBLE-CHECK LAW

beats.narration_text: Retrieval treats the problem as search, not memorization: keep documents outside the model, update them the instant they change, and cite exactly which passage answered. That's the one that actually targets the cause.

show.event: three cards land: Bigger Model, Fine-Tuning, Retrieval (RAG)
terracotta rail marks the Retrieval card as the winner

beats.narration_text: One more honest question before the close: is this always worth building? Act five: when a full retrieval pipeline is overkill.

show.event: headline types in: 'Not every problem needs a pipeline.'
spark line settles, names Act V

props.headline: Not every problem needs a pipeline.
props.subline: Sometimes the honest answer is: just paste it in.

beats.narration_text: Before I answer — predict it. What kind of knowledge base makes the entire chunk, embed, index, retrieve machinery not worth building?

show.event: question types in
underline draws
commit nudge fades in

props.question: When is RAG overkill?
props.commit: commit — the answer's one beat away

beats.narration_text: If the knowledge base is small, stable, and fits comfortably beside the question, the machinery buys almost nothing — just paste it in. The moment it outgrows a prompt, retrieval starts earning its keep.

chip 'Needs to be searched' lands
caption settles

props.caption: Small & stable vs. large & changing — the qualitative line, not a document count
props.sparkLine: Not every problem needs a pipeline.

beats.narration_text: There's no fixed document count where the line sits — practitioners disagree, and any number here would age badly. The real line is qualitative: fits in a prompt, or has to be searched.

a terracotta knob slides along the track

beats.narration_text: This time the current policy gets pulled first, and the answer on screen carries its source — the exact passage, updated eight months ago, right there to check.

beats.narration_text: Nothing about the model's reasoning changed between the wrong answer and the right one. Only its input did. That's the entire lesson: retrieve first, generate second, and the second step inherits whatever the first one found.

show.event: left frame: 'memory only' input, answer '10 sick days'
right frame: 'memory + retrieved passage' input, answer '15 sick days' in terracotta
stamp: 'only the input changed'

production_viz.label: closing comparison
production_viz.mechanic: two identical frames, only the input arrow differs
production_viz.note: mirrors the cli-explainer sibling reel's closing point

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. Every model carries a training cutoff — parametric memory, frozen at that date. RAG adds a second, non-parametric memory: real documents, searched fresh for every question, then handed to the model before it writes. A bigger model doesn't fix a stale answer; scale isn't the bottleneck. Fine-tuning updates weights but loses to retrieval at injecting fresh, citable facts, and needs retraining on every change. Retrieval earns its cost once a knowledge base outgrows what fits comfortably in a single prompt.

props.artifactHeading: The full mechanism, end to end
artifactLines: Two kinds of memory: parametric (frozen at training) and non-parametric (external, searchable, always current) — Lewis et al., 2020.
The mechanism has two separate jobs, in fixed order: retrieve, then generate — conditioned on what was found, not on memory alone.
A bigger model and fine-tuning are different KINDS of fixes — neither beats retrieval at injecting fresh, citable knowledge (Ovadia et al., 2024; Soudani et al., 2024).
Overkill when the knowledge base is small and stable enough to paste into the prompt directly.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'I have a document that changed recently, and my AI keeps answering with the old information — walk me through how RAG would fix this for MY document: what gets retrieved, what the model actually sees, and how I'd know the answer is grounded rather than remembered.' Run it on your own stale document. Watch for whether Claude names the exact passage it used — that's the whole test.
